content.text: Clouds, sunsets and lens flare on one hand; thin film, mold, chrome and crystal on the other. Cut between them on color, shape, direction and pace.
Mood board + footage library · older footage first (1920 nitrate → 1990s camcorder → today) · all clips silent · building live
Weather films, silent-era cloud studies, home-video and webcam time-lapses, park-service time-lapses. Clouds as slow fluid: heaps, rows, boiling heads, fog spilling.
The sun at the horizon from 1920 nitrate to 2008 PAL video: afterglow, red sky at morning, golden hour on rock and river.
The lens looking at the sun: flare, starburst, bloom, bokeh. Shuttle crew camcorders (1997–2001), a 640×480 sunset, 1951 Technicolor flare, aurora on video.
The sky seen from outside: ISS and shuttle passes, aurora curtains, airglow, the terminator, GOES sunrise, SDO flares. The sun up close.
Interference color: soap films, bursting and freezing bubbles, oil on a pond, the 1969 Santa Barbara slick, opal. Same physics as a halo around the sun.
Myxomycetes (Harvard, 1931), Penicillium (1952), Physarum time-lapses. Growth fronts and vein networks that move like weather.
Reflective counter-worlds: 1956 aluminum industrials, rain on metal, gallium, molten gold, ferrofluid, a 1920 mirror lake.
Crystals growing (PSSC, 1958), salt dissolving, vitamin C in polarized light, oil-and-water vortex, marbling paint on a water bath.
Palettes pulled from the footage by k-means, not picked by eye. Iridescent = four or more hue families in one shot.
Intertitles and science-film type; grain, tint, interlace and VHS bloom as surfaces.
Who looked at skies and sheens before us: Luke Howard to Stieglitz, Painlevé, Brakhage, NASA crew video.
Sky beside sheen, chosen on shared measured tags. Each pair has a named link rule.
Every catalog clip, binned by dominant color family, then screen direction, then pace.
Measured motion energy from near-static to high-velocity. Sky lane over sheen lane.
Every clip's API, license and original link. PD, CC0, CC BY and CC BY-SA only. All audio stripped.
Silent educational films (USDA "Clouds", 1920) speak in white serif caps on black, often with a border rule. Use for chapter cards: one word, held long, then the sky.
1950s–60s classroom films (PSSC, Moody Institute) set titles in plain sans or typewriter mono, often over the subject itself. Use for the sheen world: name the substance, nothing else.

The blocky on-screen date of a 1990s camcorder (e.g. "JUL 14 1995  7:42 PM") is the type of home video. Set it in a pixel mono, bottom corner, slightly bloomed. None of our clips carry one, so add it in the edit.
1920s prints: heavy grain, density flicker, scratches, sometimes amber (day) or blue (night) tints. Our USDA and Rainier clips are dark prints; let them stay dark.

Video cameras looking at the sun: highlights bloom and bleed sideways, and CCD sensors throw a vertical smear through the sun. This is the "VHS lens flare" of the brief; see the shuttle crew clips in FLARE.
Interference color is a texture, not a hue: bands that shift with thickness and angle. Read it as moving type: soap film draining top to bottom looks like a slow title crawl.
480i sources (archive camcorder, MPEG-2 rips) comb on fast motion. We deinterlaced the previews; keep the combing in finals if you want the tape feel.
Mold colonies and slime fronts are velvet, felt and vein. Shoot or pick them raking-lit so the surface reads like cloud tops seen from orbit.
Polished aluminum, mercury-like gallium and wet steel are mirrors for the sky. A sun glint on metal is the sheen world's lens flare.
"On the Modifications of Clouds": cumulus, stratus, cirrus, nimbus. The sky gets a vocabulary.
Hooke (Micrographia) and then Newton (Opticks) describe the colors of soap bubbles and thin films; Thomas Young explains them as interference in 1801–03.
Oil sketches of clouds on Hampstead Heath, each dated with the time and wind on the back.
Photographs of clouds with no horizon, meant as pictures of feeling. A model for skies with no ground in the frame.
Fleming sees mold kill a bacteria culture. The 1952 "Miracle from Mold" film in our MOLD zone tells the story.
Hollywood cinematographers (Conrad Hall, László Kovács on Easy Rider, 1969) start letting the sun flare into the lens instead of flagging it off.
A Union Oil platform blowout spreads a slick along the coast; it helps start the first Earth Day (April 22 1970). Oil sheen as a political image.
JVC launches VHS in 1976; one-piece camcorders follow in 1983–84. Home skies start arriving on tape, with bloom and smear.
Ron Fricke's cloud time-lapses pour over desert rock like water. The reference for our fastest sky clips.
Moth wings and leaves pressed directly onto film. Organic matter as light; the sheen world's art-film ancestor.
STS-81, STS-87 and STS-104 crews point camcorders at orbital sunrise: the closest public-domain thing to VHS lens flare.
Physarum, fed oat flakes placed like cities, grows a network close to the Tokyo rail system (Tero et al., Science).

props.altText: Measured palettes, one column per clip, sky above sheen

content.text: Each column is one clip: its six k-means colors stacked by weight, with the primary family as the bar underneath. Sky (A) on top, sheen (B) below, ordered by family.

Minutes by family (A / B): silver-gray 2.8/6.5 · void-black 4.9/2.8 · sky-blue 4.3/1.1 · gold 0.8/2.8 · cyan 1.6/0.6 · sunset-orange 1.8/1.0 · mold-green 1.3/0.2 · iridescent 0.0/2.0 · flare-red 0.3/0.5 · magenta 0.0/0.1

Reading it: the old film is gray and black in both worlds, which is the strongest bridge. Color lives in sunsets and SDO on the sky side and in thin film, molten metal and Physarum on the sheen side. Cut gray to gray, then let a hue lock carry you into color.

Seventeen cuts from sky into sheen. Each has a named link rule (hue lock, direction carry, shape rhyme, pace match…), picked on shared measured tags and checked by eye. Left is A · sky, right is B · sheen. Play both and cut on the rule.

content.text: Pace measured from motion energy: pace_raw = 0.6 × median optical flow + 0.4 × 90th-percentile flow (px/s at 160 px width, Farneback, 6 fps). Board-relative steps: 1 <2 · 2 2–5 · 3 5–10 · 4 10–17 · 5 ≥17 (this library is slower than street footage; on the Chicago 1993 scale, 3/9/17/25, it would sit one step lower), checked by eye on the extremes; film flicker and grain can add a little to old prints. Each lane runs 1 → 5 left to right, ordered by the raw value.
